'''Shaun Wylie''' (17 January 1913 – 2 October 2009<ref name=death>[https://web.archive.org/web/20100523202355/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/comment/obituaries/article6903467.ece Obituary — Shaun Wylie: member of Bletchley Park code-breaking team], ''[[The Times]]'', 5 November 2009.</ref><ref name="trin">[http://www.trinhall.cam.ac.uk/news/article.asp?ItemID=1205 Dr Shaun Wylie, 1913–2009] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303210318/http://www.trinhall.cam.ac.uk/news/article.asp?ItemID=1205 |date=3 March 2016 }}, [[Trinity Hall, Cambridge]], UK.</ref>) was a British [[mathematician]] and [[World War II]] codebreaker.

==Early life==
Wylie was born in [[Oxford]], [[England]]. The fourth son of [[Francis James Wylie|Sir Francis Wylie]] (later the first Warden of [[Rhodes House]],<ref>[http://www.rhodeshouse.ox.ac.uk/page/deaths Deaths] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131021034213/http://www.rhodeshouse.ox.ac.uk/page/deaths |date=21 October 2013 }}, Rhodes House Trust, Oxford, UK.</ref> Oxford) and his wife Kathleen (formerly Kelly), he was educated at the [[Dragon School]] (in Oxford) and then [[Winchester College]].<ref name="int">[https://www.princeton.edu/~mudd/finding_aids/mathoral/pmc45.htm An interview with Shaun Wylie] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150310074640/http://www.princeton.edu/~mudd/finding_aids/mathoral/pmc45.htm |date=10 March 2015 }} on 21 June 1985, The Princeton Mathematics Community in the 1930s, Transcript Number 45 (PMC<!-- Not a PMCID --> 5).</ref> He won a scholarship to [[New College, Oxford]] where he studied mathematics and [[Literae Humaniores|classics]].<ref name="int"/> In 1934, he went to study [[topology]] at [[Princeton University]], obtaining a PhD in 1937 with [[Solomon Lefschetz]] as his supervisor.<ref name="gen">{{MathGenealogy|1406}}</ref> At Princeton he met fellow English mathematician [[Alan Turing]].<ref name="int"/> He became a fellow of [[Trinity Hall, Cambridge]] in 1938/1939.<ref name="trin"/><ref name="trin-newsletter-2005">[http://www.trinhall.cam.ac.uk/uploads/TH%20NL%20Spring%202005.pdf Trinity Hall Newsletter] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607175104/http://www.trinhall.cam.ac.uk/uploads/TH%20NL%20Spring%202005.pdf |date=7 June 2011 }}, Spring 2005.</ref>

==World War II codebreaking==
[[File:Enigma rotors and spindle showing contacts rachet and notch.jpg|thumb|left|Wylie contributed to the breaking of the [[Enigma machine]] code.]]
During [[World War II]], Turing had been recruited to work at [[Bletchley Park]], Britain's codebreaking centre. Turing wrote to Wylie around December 1940, who was by then teaching at [[Wellington College, Berkshire|Wellington College]], inviting him to work at Bletchley Park.<ref name="hodges198">[[Andrew Hodges]], ''[[Alan Turing: The Enigma]]'', [[Simon & Schuster]], 1983, p. 198</ref> He accepted, and arrived in February 1941.<ref name="hodges198"/> He joined Turing's section, [[Hut 8]], which was working on solving the [[Enigma machine]] as used by the ''[[Kriegsmarine]]''. He became head of the [[crib (cryptanalysis)|crib]] subsection,<ref>Michael Smith, ''Station X'', revised edition 2004, p. 117</ref> and allocated time on the [[bombe]] codebreaking machines.<ref>Ralph Erskine, 2001, p. 58</ref>
[[Conel Hugh O'Donel Alexander|Hugh Alexander]], successor to Turing as head of Hut 8, commented that "except for Turing, no-one made a bigger contribution to the success of Hut 8 than Shaun Wylie; he was astonishingly quick and resourceful and contributed to theory and practice in a number of different directions".<ref>[http://www.bletchleypark.org.uk/content/archive/oct1943.rhtm "Not all our own way"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130402205420/http://www.bletchleypark.org.uk/content/archive/oct1943.rhtm |date=2 April 2013 }}, Bletchley Park History, "Articles from our archives", http://www.bletchleypark.org.uk, retrieved 12 October 2009</ref>

Wylie transferred in Autumn 1943 to work on "[[Lorenz cipher|Tunny]]", a [[Germany|German]] teleprinter cipher.<ref>Wylie, 2001, p. 318</ref> He married Odette Murray, a [[Women's Royal Naval Service|WREN]] in the section.<ref>Smith, 2004, pp. 159-160</ref> In 1945, soon after the [[victory in Europe]], Wylie demonstrated how [[Colossus computer|Colossus]] – electronic machines used to help solve Tunny – could have been used unmodified to break the Tunny "motor wheels", a task which had been previously done by hand.<ref>Randall, 2006, p. 148</ref> While at Bletchley Park, he became president of the dramatic club.<ref name="kahn">Kahn, 1991, pp. 137-138</ref> He had also played international [[field hockey|hockey]] for [[Scotland]],<ref name="kahn"/> but according to fellow codebreaker [[I. J. Good]], he "never mentioned any of his successes".<ref name="good206">Good, 2006, p. 209</ref>

==Post-war==
{{Moresources|section|date=December 2022}}
After the war, he was a fellow at Trinity Hall until 1958<ref name="trin"/> and lectured in mathematics.<ref name="atd-note">"Notes on contributors", p. 532 in Michael Smith and Ralph Erskine, editors, ''Action This Day'', 2001</ref> He was the [[PhD]] advisor for [[Frank Adams]], [[Max Kelly]], [[Crispin St. J. A. Nash-Williams|Crispin Nash-Williams]], [[William Tutte]] and [[Christopher Zeeman]].<ref name="gen"/> With [[Peter Hilton]], he authored ''Homology Theory: An Introduction to Algebraic Topology'', published in 1960.<ref name="good206"/>

In 1958, he became Chief Mathematician at [[GCHQ]], the UK [[signals intelligence]] organisation.<ref name="gen"/> In July 1969, he was sent a draft paper by [[James H. Ellis]], another GCHQ mathematician, about the possibility of what was termed "non-secret encryption", or what is now more commonly known as [[public-key cryptography]], on which Wylie commented "unfortunately, I can't see anything wrong with this".<ref name="levy">Steven Levy, ''Crypto'', 2001, p. 318</ref> He retired in 1973, and taught at [[Cambridgeshire High School for Boys]] (later [[Hills Road Sixth Form College]]) in Cambridge for seven years.<ref name="gen"/> He was elected an [[Honorary title (academic)|honorary fellow]] at Trinity Hall in 1980.<ref name="trin"/>

Wylie supervised five PhD students at Cambridge, through whom he had over 1600 "descendants" in 2021 according to the [[American Mathematical Society]] [[Mathematical Genealogy Project]].<ref name="gen"/> In addition he influenced the intellectual development of generations of pupils at the [[Cambridgeshire High School for Boys]]/[[Hills Road Sixth Form College]] where he taught maths (including statistics, with his beloved chi-squared distribution) and classical Greek and where he also produced plays (such as [[Anton Chekov|Chekhov]]'s ''[[The Cherry Orchard]]'') and supervised the school chess team. He also came out of retirement temporarily to teach Mathematics at Long Road Sixth Form College.

After retirement from teaching, Wylie was instrumental in the founding of the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]] and in the Cambridge-based [[University of the Third Age]] and at the time of his death was preparing to read in the next [[Cambridge Greek Play]], [[Aeschylus]]' ''[[Agamemnon (play)|Agamemnon]]''.

His eldest son, the late [[Keith Wylie]] (1945–1999), a [[barrister]], was a [[croquet]] international and open champion of Great Britain.<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20100729105841/http://www.mauicroquetclub.org/people/KeithWylie.htm Keith Wylie Dead at 54]}}, ''[[The Times]]'', 1999.</ref> His second son Malcolm (b1949) pioneered the walk from John o'Groats to Land's End along the [[British watershed|British Watershed]] between 1996 and 2009.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wylie |first=Malcolm |title=Walking the British Watershed |date=11 December 2025 |publisher=Brown Dog Books |isbn=978-1-83952-989-4}}</ref>

Shaun Wylie died on 2 October 2009, aged 96.<ref name=death /><ref name="trin"/>
